title: I built a multiplayer experiment where AI enemies learn and evolve across sessions
author: SoClassDD
selftext:
Hey Community,

I’ve just launched [EvoGoo](https://evogoo.com/), a multiplayer browser experiment where AI sentinels evolve in real-time as people play. I honestly just want to see how strong they can become haha! 😄

Five years ago, I built a Pygame project showcasing NEAT (NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies, originally introduced by Kenneth Stanley and Risto Miikkulainen). To bring it to the web, I used Codex to help port and restructure that legacy codebase into a multiplayer browser game.

While Codex was incredible for translating the core genetic algorithm and neural network loops, it definitely struggled with the visual feedback loop. Specifically, I ran into major headaches trying to get walking and running animations to look natural without awkward foot sliding. Do you have any tips to make them better?

# Two Modes to Explore:

* **Survival:** Stay alive as long as possible. Sentinels evolve to chase players, close gaps, and navigate obstacles.
* **Motion Hunt:** Grab a life-support seed and reach the exit. Sentinels evolve to detect movement, target players, and hunt relentlessly. (Timing is everything. Knowing when to move or stay still is key, well at least in theory 😂).

# How the Experiment Works:

* **Multiplayer Arenas:** Up to 12 players share each arena, collectively shaping the challenges the sentinels face.
* **Persistent Evolution:** Progress carries forward across sessions. Every player contributes to what the population becomes. Better hunters? Or worse? That is part of the fun.
* **Genetic Networks:** Each mode evolves its own population. Successful sentinels pass on their neural networks, with mutations creating new variations for the next generation.

I would love for you to drop in, test it out, and share your thoughts on the neuroevolution behavior loops, the visuals and the animation!

#

replies.author: SoClassDD
replies.body:
Well, I like the world design. It's a bit simplistic, but it should be enough for this experiment for now.   
  
As for the walking and running animations... not really. I've tried so many iterations and I'm still not satisfied.
